name: Head-Hair Boundary Analysis
description: Analyzes the boundary quality between head and hair regions — AI often produces unnatural hairline rendering.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated or manipulated faces by analyzing the boundary between skin and hair regions, which is extremely difficult for generators to render naturally:

1. **Hairline Segmentation and Boundary Extraction**: The method uses face parsing networks (BiSeNet, FARL) to segment the face into semantic regions including skin, hair, and background. The hair-skin boundary (hairline) is extracted as a contour — the curve where hair region meets skin region along the forehead, temples, and sideburn areas. Real hairlines have characteristic properties: they consist of individual hair strands that create a gradual density transition from skin to full hair coverage over a width of 3–8 mm (approximately 10–30 pixels at typical face resolution). This transition zone is critical — real hairlines are never sharp binary boundaries.

2. **Transition Zone Analysis**: The method analyzes the pixel intensity gradient profile perpendicular to the hairline boundary. In real faces, the transition from skin to hair follows a sigmoidal profile with a characteristic width determined by strand density, hair color, and hair type. The method fits a sigmoid function I(x) = A / (1 + exp(-k(x - x₀))) + B to the perpendicular intensity profile and measures: (a) transition width (1/k) — real hairlines have width 5–25 pixels, (b) symmetry — real transitions may be slightly asymmetric (more gradual on the skin side due to vellus hair), (c) consistency — the transition profile should be similar along the entire hairline length. AI-generated faces often produce hairlines that are too sharp (1–3 pixel transition, like a mask edge), too uniform, or have varying transition widths along the boundary.

3. **Individual Strand Visibility**: At the hairline of real faces, individual hair strands are visible as semi-transparent wisps against the skin. These strands create a stochastic edge pattern — random, naturally varying strand positions and angles. The method analyzes the high-frequency content along the hairline using Gabor filters tuned to detect strand-like structures (thin, elongated, oriented approximately perpendicular to the hairline). Real hairlines show strong Gabor responses with natural orientation variation (20–40° range). AI-generated hairlines typically show either no individual strand detail (smooth boundary) or artificially regular strand patterns (too uniform spacing, identical angles).

4. **Temporal Hairline Stability in Video**: In video, the hairline boundary should remain anatomically fixed — it moves only with head motion and does not change shape (hairline shape is determined by follicle positions, which are permanent). The method tracks the hairline contour across frames, normalizing for head pose changes using 3DMM fitting. The Hausdorff distance between normalized hairline contours across frames should be < 3 pixels for authentic video. Deepfakes often show hairline instability — the boundary shifts, its shape changes, or the transition zone width varies between frames because the generator produces the hairline independently each frame.
parameters:
Face parsing: BiSeNet / FARL semantic segmentation
Hairline extraction: contour between hair and skin labels
Transition profile: sigmoid fit I(x) = A/(1+exp(-k(x-x₀)))+B
Transition width: 1/k, expected 5–25 pixels
Gabor strand detection: 6 orientations, 2 scales
Strand orientation variation: expected 20–40° range
Temporal tracking: 3DMM-normalized hairline contour
Hausdorff distance threshold: < 3 pixels between frames
Minimum face resolution: 128×128 pixels
accuracy: 80–88% accuracy detecting AI-generated faces via hairline analysis. Transition zone analysis achieves AUC of 0.86 for GAN-generated faces. Individual strand visibility check provides F1-score of 0.83. Temporal hairline stability achieves AUC of 0.89 in video analysis. Performance is strongest for hairlines visible against skin background (receding hairlines, ponytails) and weakest for bangs that cover the forehead.
source: Neves, J. C. et al. (2020). GANprintr: Improved Fakes and Evaluation of the State of the Art in Face Manipulation Detection. IEEE JSTSP, 14(5), 1038–1048.
useCase: Detecting face swap deepfakes through hairline boundary analysis. Identifying AI-generated face portraits via unnatural hairline rendering. Forensic analysis of face compositing quality. Supplementary signal for multi-modal deepfake detection.
strengths:
• Hairline is one of the most consistently problematic regions for AI generators
• Transition zone analysis provides quantitative measurement of boundary quality
• Individual strand visibility is extremely difficult to synthesize correctly
• Temporal stability provides strong video-specific detection signal
• Works independently of face generation method
limitations:
• Bangs, hats, or headwear cover the hairline, eliminating the signal
• Bald or shaved heads have minimal hairline to analyze
• Dark hair against dark skin reduces transition zone contrast
• High-quality generators (StyleGAN3) are improving hairline rendering
• Heavy compression destroys fine strand-level detail
